title: IRS Interest Rate Rises to 8 Percent on January 1: Price Every IRS Balance Against Your Bank Line, Pay the January 15 Estimate Before the Penalty Reprices, and Book Tax, Interest, and Penalty as a Draw, Not an Expense
excerpt: The IRS interest rate for individuals goes from 7 percent to 8 percent on January 1, 2027, compounded daily, and the 2026 estimated tax penalty runs at the new rate from that day until a short installment is paid. Here is what an IRS balance costs once the failure-to-pay penalty stacks on top, how that compares with a bank line or a card, what a missed September installment costs if paid in December, January, or April, and why a sole proprietor books the tax, the interest, and the penalty as a draw rather than an expense.
author: FinBoard Team
coverAlt: Small business owner's worksheet for the IRS interest rate increase to 8 percent on January 1, 2027, listing each IRS balance with its daily interest and penalty, the bank line comparison, the January 15 estimate, and the owner's draw entry
content:
The IRS interest rate rises from 7 percent to 8 percent on January 1, 2027, and 8 percent also applies to the estimated tax penalty on any 2026 installment unpaid after that date. Before the quarter turns, price every IRS balance against your other borrowing, pay the January 15 estimate, and book tax, interest, and penalty on separate lines.

Why the IRS interest rate matters now

The IRS announced the change in IR-2026-144, published 2026-11-24. For the calendar quarter beginning January 1, 2027, the rate for individual overpayments and underpayments will be 8 percent per year, compounded daily. Corporations will pay 8 percent on underpayments and 10 percent on large corporate underpayments, and will receive 7 percent on overpayments, with 5.5 percent on the portion of a corporate overpayment above $10,000. The release explains that the rate 'is determined on a quarterly basis,' that for taxpayers other than corporations it is 'the federal short-term rate plus 3 percentage points,' and that the new rates were computed from the federal short-term rate determined during October 2026. Revenue Ruling 2026-25, which carries the rates, will appear in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2026-51 on December 14, 2026.

The IRS quarterly interest rates table, updated 2026-09-10, shows the path here: 7 percent for individuals in every quarter of 2025, a dip to 6 percent in the second quarter of 2026, and 7 percent since July. January's 8 percent is the highest the rate has been since 2024. Two rules on the IRS interest page, updated 2026-04-26, decide what that means for money you already owe: 'Interest will continue to accrue daily on any amount not paid, including on both penalties and interest,' and 'Changes don't affect the interest rate charged for prior quarters or years.' A balance from 2024 keeps its 7 percent history and starts costing 8 percent on January 1.

The change lands on two deadlines. The fourth 2026 estimated tax installment is due January 15, 2027, per the IRS estimated tax schedule, updated 2026-10-02. And the penalty for underpaying 2026 estimates, which the IRS underpayment penalty page, updated 2026-08-20, says is computed from 'the amount of the underpayment,' 'the period when the underpayment was due and underpaid,' and 'the published quarterly interest rates for underpayments,' will run at 8 percent for every day from January 1 to April 15, 2027 that a 2026 installment stays short.

Coverage so far reports the rates. A back-tax explainer updated 2026-11-21, IRS interest rate 2027, said the first-quarter rate had not yet been announced and advised paying balances down before January. Business-owner coverage of the release says to close the books, set cash aside, and pay on January 15. None of it prices the full stack of interest, failure-to-pay penalty, and interest on the penalty against a bank line or a card, works out what a missed September installment costs if paid in December, January, or April, or says where the tax, the interest, and the penalty belong in a sole proprietor's books. That is what follows.

What an IRS balance actually costs after January 1

Three charges run on an unpaid federal balance, and each is computed differently.

Interest. Topic 653, updated 2026-11-09, puts it in two words: 'Interest compounds daily.' At 8 percent the daily rate is 8 divided by 365, about 0.0219 percent, and daily compounding turns a stated 8 percent into about 8.33 percent over a full year. At 7 percent the same math gives about 7.25 percent. Interest starts on the due date of the amount owed and stops when the balance is paid in full. On a $9,000 balance the increase is worth about 25 cents a day, roughly $90 a year. The rate change alone is not the expensive part.

The failure-to-pay penalty. The IRS failure to pay penalty page, updated 2026-11-16, sets it at '0.5% of the unpaid taxes for each month or part of a month the tax remains unpaid,' capped at 25 percent of the unpaid tax. Two adjustments matter to an owner. 'If you filed your tax return on time as an individual and you have an approved payment plan, the failure to pay penalty is reduced to 0.25% per month (or partial month).' And 'If you don't pay your tax in 10 days after getting a notice from us with our intent to levy, the failure to pay penalty is 1% per month or partial month.' Then the line most people skip: 'We charge interest on penalties.' So the penalty is 6 percent a year with no plan, 3 percent on a plan, 12 percent after a levy notice, and each month's penalty starts earning 8 percent interest of its own. That is the expensive part.

The estimated tax penalty. This one is not compounded. The Form 2210 instructions, updated 2026-04-30, say the penalty 'is figured for the number of days that each underpayment remains unpaid,' period by period, at the quarterly rate in force during each rate period. For a 2026 return the periods run from each installment's due date through December 31, 2026 at 7 percent, then from January 1, 2027 to April 15, 2027 at 8 percent, and the clock on an installment stops the day it is paid. There is no monthly penalty stacked on top, and no interest on the penalty until the return's own balance goes unpaid after April 15.

Put the three together and set them beside the other places an owner borrows. The bank line and card rates in the table are illustrative; read your own statements. The deductibility column follows a Treasury regulation, 26 CFR 1.163-9T, which treats as personal interest any interest paid on underpayments of individual federal, state, or local income taxes 'and on indebtedness used to pay such taxes,' and does so 'regardless of the source of the income generating the tax liability.' The Tax Court upheld that rule for a business owner in Robinson, 119 TC No. 4 (2002). Penalties paid to a government are not deductible by anyone.

One studio, three IRS balances, one December: the walk-through

Call her Priya Castellanos. She runs a two-person design studio as a sole proprietor, keeps the books in QuickBooks Online, and files a Schedule C. The figures are illustrative; the sequence is the point.

Step one: list every IRS balance with its own clock

Her 2025 return showed $31,000 of total tax on $140,000 of adjusted gross income, so her 2026 safe harbor is 100 percent of last year's tax, in four installments of $7,750. She paid April 15 and June 15. She skipped September 15 when a client paid 60 days late. She also still owes $9,000 of 2024 tax on a direct-debit payment plan at $400 a month, approved in July 2025 after she filed that return on time. The register has three rows: the missed third installment of $7,750, due 2026-09-15; the fourth installment of $7,750, due 2027-01-15; and the 2024 balance, with the payoff amount pulled from her IRS online account on the day she looks, because accrued interest and penalty are already in it. If a CP53E notice had turned a credited 2025 overpayment into a refund, that would be a fourth row, and the register would start from the transcript instead.

Step two: price the missed September installment three ways

The penalty on the $7,750 runs day by day. September 15 to December 31 is 107 days at 7 percent: $7,750 times 0.07 times 107 divided by 365, or $159. If she pays on December 1, the clock stops at 77 days and the penalty is $114. If she pays with the fourth installment on January 15, she adds 15 days at 8 percent, about $25, for a total near $185. If she waits for the return on April 15, she adds 105 days at 8 percent, about $178, for a total near $337. The rate change costs her nothing if the money goes out before January 1 and about $150 if she waits until April. She has the cash from November's invoices. She pays on December 1.

Step three: compare the 2024 payment plan with the bank line

On the $9,000 balance the IRS charges 7 percent compounded daily now, about $1.73 a day, rising to $1.97 a day in January, plus the reduced 0.25 percent monthly penalty, $22.50 a month, plus interest on that penalty. Over a year that is roughly $750 of interest and $270 of penalty, about 11.3 percent all in. Her bank line costs 9.5 percent on the drawn balance, about $855 a year on $9,000, with no penalty. The line is cheaper by around $165 a year, and paying off the IRS stops the penalty from climbing toward its 25 percent cap. Two things don't change when she draws on the line. The interest on the draw is still personal interest, because the regulation covers 'indebtedness used to pay such taxes,' so it is not a Schedule C deduction. And the IRS balance was never the business's debt, so the $9,000 that leaves the business account is her draw. She pulls the payoff figure from her online account, draws $9,000 plus the accrued charges, pays the IRS the same day, and confirms the monthly direct debit has stopped. The business card, at 24 percent plus the processor's fee, stays where it was: last.

Step four: size the January 15 installment from the books

Her books through November show 2026 net profit of $118,000, ahead of 2025's $104,000, so 2026 tax will be higher than $31,000. The safe harbor is still 100 percent of 2025 tax because her 2025 adjusted gross income was under $150,000. To be fully paid in for 2026 she needs $31,000 in by January 15: $15,500 already paid, $7,750 paid December 1 for the third installment, and $7,750 due January 15. Anything owed above $31,000 is due April 15 with the return, with no estimated tax penalty on it. She moves $7,750 to a separate tax account now and pays on January 15 through her IRS online account, keeping the confirmation so the payment can be matched to the bank feed. The monthly profit figure that drives all of this is one of the five numbers worth checking every month, not something to rebuild in April.

Step five: fix the entries

The $400 plan debits for January through November, $4,400 in total, had been posted to Taxes and Licenses. Her income tax, the interest on it, and the penalty on it are personal, so the entry is debit Owner's Draw $4,400, credit Taxes and Licenses $4,400. Net profit goes up by $4,400 and Schedule C stops carrying a deduction she was never entitled to. The line draw is debit Cash, credit Line of Credit for the amount borrowed. The payoff is debit Owner's Draw, credit Cash for the full amount paid to the IRS, with the tax, interest, and penalty noted in the memo so each can be traced to the IRS notice. The December 1 and January 15 estimates are debit Owner's Draw, credit Cash. When the 2026 return is filed, the small estimated tax penalty is a draw too.

The entity changes the accounts, not the rule. An S corporation or partnership doesn't owe the owner's income tax either, so the same payments are shareholder or partner distributions. A C corporation owns its tax: debit Income Tax Expense, credit Income Taxes Payable when the liability is known, debit Interest Expense for IRS interest, which a corporation can deduct, and a separate Penalties account for the nondeductible penalty so the book-to-tax adjustment stays visible. Late payroll tax deposits belong to the business in every entity type; book the interest and the penalty in the business, on separate lines, and treat the penalty as nondeductible. Owners who keep the books with a firm's help can put this rule into the monthly bookkeeping scope so no IRS payment reaches an expense account by default.

Time: half an hour to build the register, half an hour on the three prices, twenty minutes on the payoff decision, fifteen minutes on the reclass. The alternative was a 2026 Schedule C overstating expenses by $4,400, a penalty clock running at the new rate into April, and a plan balance costing more than the bank line.

Accounting controls for the IRS balance review

Source data: the IRS online account balance and payoff amount, dated; the 2025 return's total tax and adjusted gross income; each 2026 installment paid, with date and confirmation number; the payment plan's approval date, monthly amount, and whether the return was filed on time; the bank line and card statements showing current rates; the books through the latest closed month; and the dated IRS pages relied on, including IR-2026-144 published 2026-11-24, the failure to pay penalty page updated 2026-11-16, and Topic 653 updated 2026-11-09.

Calculation: a fixed sequence anyone can rerun. The required annual payment is the smaller of 90 percent of projected 2026 tax or 100 percent of 2025 tax, 110 percent when 2025 adjusted gross income exceeded $150,000, divided into four installments. The shortfall at each due date is the cumulative requirement minus cumulative payments, floored at zero. The estimated tax penalty on each shortfall is the shortfall times days unpaid divided by 365 times the period rate, 7 percent for days through December 31, 2026 and 8 percent for days from January 1, 2027, stopping on the payment date or April 15, 2027. Interest on an assessed balance is the annual rate divided by 365, compounded daily on tax, penalty, and prior interest. The failure-to-pay penalty is 0.5 percent of unpaid tax per month, 0.25 percent while an approved plan is in effect and the return was filed on time, 1 percent after a levy notice, capped at 25 percent. All-in IRS cost equals effective interest plus the annualized penalty rate, compared with the line and card rates on the statements. For a sole proprietor every income tax, interest, and penalty payment is debit Owner's Draw, credit Cash.

Review: a second person, the bookkeeper or the preparer, confirms that every IRS payment in the bank feed for the year is posted to draw and none to an expense account, that the payoff figure used matches the online account on the payoff date, that the estimated tax penalty uses the right day counts and rate periods, that the plan's direct debit stopped after payoff, and that the line draw and the IRS payment are two entries, not one netted entry. Any balance the owner can't see in the online account is an open item, not a presumed zero.

Decision: the owner owns the pay-now, pay-in-January, or pay-in-April choice for each balance and the borrow-to-pay decision, and documents the rate comparison. The preparer owns the safe harbor choice and Form 2210, including Schedule AI when income arrived unevenly during the year. The bookkeeper owns the reclass and the memo on each payment. Nobody books an IRS notice as one line.

Limits and common mistakes

The rates here are for the first quarter of 2027 only. The IRS sets them quarterly, and the second-quarter rate will be announced in early 2027. The studio, its owner, and every figure are illustrative, and the bank line and card rates are placeholders for your own statements. State tax agencies set their own interest and penalty rules. Waivers of the estimated tax penalty exist for casualty, disaster, and other unusual circumstances, and Form 2210 governs the computation.

Don't compare 8 percent to your line's rate and stop. The failure-to-pay penalty and the interest on it are the larger cost.

Don't assume borrowing from the business to pay personal income tax makes the interest deductible. The regulation reaches debt used to pay the tax.

Don't post an IRS income tax payment to Taxes and Licenses or Interest Expense in a sole proprietorship, partnership, or S corporation. It is a draw or a distribution, and leaving it in expenses understates profit and misstates the return.

Don't net an IRS notice into one line. Tax, interest, and penalty have different deductibility and different clocks.

Don't wait for April to pay a missed installment. The clock runs at 8 percent from January 1 until the day it is paid.

Don't let a payment plan default while deciding. The IRS says a reinstatement fee may apply, and the reduced penalty rate only applies for months in which the agreement is in effect.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the IRS interest rate for the first quarter of 2027?

For the quarter beginning January 1, 2027, the IRS rate for individual overpayments and underpayments is 8 percent per year, compounded daily, up from 7 percent in the fourth quarter of 2026. Corporations pay 8 percent on underpayments and 10 percent on large corporate underpayments, and receive 7 percent on overpayments, with 5.5 percent on the portion of an overpayment above $10,000. The IRS announced the rates in IR-2026-144 on November 24, 2026.

Does the 8 percent rate apply to a tax balance I already owe from an earlier year?

Yes, for every day from January 1, 2027 until the balance is paid. The IRS says rate changes don't affect the interest charged for prior quarters, so the days before January 1 keep their 7 percent rate. Interest compounds daily on the unpaid tax, on penalties, and on interest already charged, and the failure-to-pay penalty keeps running separately until the balance is paid in full.

Does the increase change the penalty for underpaying 2026 estimated tax?

Yes, for the days from January 1, 2027 to the earlier of the payment date or April 15, 2027. The estimated tax penalty is figured for the number of days each installment stays unpaid, using the quarterly underpayment rate in force during each rate period, so days through December 31, 2026 are charged at 7 percent and days after that at 8 percent. Paying a missed installment sooner shortens the clock.

Can a sole proprietor deduct interest paid to the IRS on an income tax underpayment?

No. Treasury regulation 1.163-9T treats interest on underpayments of individual federal, state, or local income taxes, and interest on money borrowed to pay those taxes, as personal interest regardless of the source of the income that produced the tax, and the Tax Court upheld that rule for a business owner in 2002. Penalties paid to a government are not deductible for anyone. A C corporation can deduct the interest but not the penalty.

Should I borrow from my business line of credit to pay off an IRS payment plan?

Compare the all-in cost. An IRS balance on an approved plan costs about 8.3 percent after daily compounding plus a 0.25 percent per month failure-to-pay penalty, roughly 11 to 12 percent a year, and about 14 to 15 percent without a plan. If your line is cheaper, paying off the IRS saves money, but the line's interest is still personal interest when the loan pays your income tax, and the payment is an owner's draw in the books, not a business expense. Get the payoff amount from your IRS online account on the day you pay.

Once every IRS balance sits in one register with its clock, its all-in rate, and its entry, the owner can see in December what the April return would otherwise reveal: which payments were posted to expense, which installment is short, and which balance costs more than the bank. FinBoard connects your QuickBooks Online file and shows net profit by month and every payment to the IRS by account, so an owner or their bookkeeper can find the ones posted to expense and drill to the transaction before the return is prepared.
